records.subject: fix(sairndental): a failed booking left a patient record the practice cannot delete
records.summary: api/sairndental/public-book.js wrote a dnt_patients row before the appointment it exists for, and a failed booking left that patient record behind with no route to remove it -- on an unauthenticated public endpoint, so an anonymous caller could accumulate them. PHI created by a transaction that did not complete, in a practice that cannot delete it.

injection.unknown_reason: The orphan is a consequence of the booking endpoint's ordering, which has been its shape since the endpoint was written; no single commit introduced the missing rollback, so blaming one would be a guess dressed as a fact.

records.citation_note: No standing rule covers 'a partial write on a failure path leaves a record the owner cannot remove'. The nearest is the removal-path work on the SAIRNbiz pair, which is about a MISSING verb rather than about an orphan created by a failed transaction.
records.phase_note: Read from the fix: a patient row is written before the appointment that justifies it, with no compensating delete on the failure path. An ordering decision, not a coding slip.

contributing_factors.factor: The patient row was written BEFORE the appointment it exists for, so every booking that then failed left an orphan. The most common failure is the 409 slot race two people hit on purpose by clicking the same popular time.
contributing_factors.action: the order is reversed -- claim the SLOT first, write the patient only once it is secured, so a 409 or a 502 leaves no trace.

contributing_factors.factor: The patient write was a bare `await fetch(...)` whose result was never checked. On failure patientId still pointed at a row that did not exist and the appointment was written referencing a PHANTOM PATIENT, reported as a clean 200.
contributing_factors.action: the result is checked and the response carries patient_record: 'saved' | 'not_saved'.
contributing_factors.note: This is the same write-path shape as cluster 5b98fd27: a call whose result nobody reads, reported as success.

contributing_factors.factor: CLEANING UP AFTERWARDS WAS NEVER AVAILABLE AS A FIX. dnt_patients has no delete grant -- revoked platform-wide by sql/unused_delete_grant_revoke_2026-08-24.sql -- so the debris is permanent PHI in a dental record system and no remediation path existed.
contributing_factors.note: The revoke is correct and is not being undone. What it means is that any write which can create an orphan is unrecoverable by construction, so the ordering fix is the only available class of fix. Recorded so a future session does not reach for a cleanup that cannot exist.

contributing_factors.factor: The endpoint is PUBLIC AND UNAUTHENTICATED, so anyone able to load the booking page could mint unbounded rows carrying name, date of birth, phone and email just by racing a slot or retrying a failing one. Nothing bounded the rate or the volume.
contributing_factors.note: The ordering fix removes the orphan, not the exposure of an unauthenticated write path to a PHI table. That is a wider question than this defect and is not closed here.

contributing_factors.factor: The open-work row named ONE of the two defects. The phantom-patient write was found only by reading the code while fixing the first, not by the process that recorded it.
contributing_factors.note: Not actioned as a process change here. It is the argument for tools/optimistic_success_scan.py, which looks for exactly this shape -- a dropped write and a success reported anyway -- across the platform rather than one site at a time.

records.recurrence_open: NOT CLOSED FOR THE CLASS. The ordering fix is specific to this endpoint. records.subject: fix(sairnlaw,platform): the advisory lock was doing nothing under REPEATABLE READ -- on attorney trust money, and in two other places
records.summary: law_check_and_insert_disbursement holds an advisory lock while summing the trust balance and then inserting, with nothing requiring READ COMMITTED. pg_advisory_xact_lock serialises ACQUISITION and not the SNAPSHOT, so under REPEATABLE READ two concurrent disbursements against one client each sum a balance from before the other committed, both pass the sufficiency check, and both insert -- an overdrawn IOLTA client trust ledger with the lock held correctly throughout. Not exploitable on the current deployment, which uses the default isolation; one ALTER ROLE statement away, and that statement reads as a hardening change.

Forcing 1.11 would manufacture agreement the matcher would then score.
records.phase_note: Read from the function body: the lock, the aggregate and the insert are all present and correct; what is absent is the isolation precondition they rest on. A design-time omission, not a coding slip.

contributing_factors.factor: pg_advisory_xact_lock serialises ACQUISITION, not the SNAPSHOT. Under REPEATABLE READ a caller that waited on the lock still reads from before the holder committed, so read-decide-write is not atomic however correctly the lock is used.

contributing_factors.factor: THE CODE CONTAINING THE BUG IS CORRECT. The thing that is wrong is a setting in another file -- one ALTER ROLE away -- and that statement reads as a HARDENING change. There is no defect visible at the site to review.

contributing_factors.action: the sweep was run across all nine advisory-lock functions and the checker now runs on every invocation.

contributing_factors.action: the comment is now backed by the checker, so the claim and the enforcement move together.

records.subject: fix(tests): two arms of mine were about my habits, not the register's rules
records.summary: Two arms in tests/run_capa_fields_probe.py encoded their author's habits as rules and failed another session's correct records: one demanded the literal phrase 'NOT CLOSED' in recurrence_open, the other demanded contributing factors span more than one kind, which tools/defect_register.py does not require. A control that fails a correct record for a rule the tool does not enforce trains authors to copy a string rather than say what is open.

records.citation_note: No standing rule names 'a control encoding its author's style as a requirement'. The nearest is the platform's refusal of word lists, which is stated in tool headers rather than in the process rules, so citing a section would be inventing one.
records.phase_note: Both arms were written correct-looking against the only records that existed at the time, which were the author's own.

contributing_factors.factor: An arm required the LITERAL string 'NOT CLOSED' in recurrence_open, which is how its author happens to write them. Another session stated the residual in its own words and the probe failed a correct record.
contributing_factors.action: the arm now asserts the PROPERTY -- states a residual, does not dismiss one -- rather than a wording.

contributing_factors.factor: A second arm required contributing factors to span more than one KIND. tools/defect_register.py requires no such thing, so the probe was failing another author's record for a rule the TOOL does not enforce.
contributing_factors.action: demoted to a printed count. If single-kind records should be refused, that belongs in cmd_check where every author sees it.

contributing_factors.note: The class is not closed. Every probe over a shared register or document has the same exposure, and nothing distinguishes 'this is the rule' from 'this is how I write it' at the point the arm is authored. The only thing that surfaced it here was a second author.

contributing_factors.factor: A word list decides nothing correctly in either direction, and this platform refuses word lists everywhere else -- optimistic_success_scan.py has an arm whose entire purpose is that no word list decides whether a message reads as success. contributing_factors.note: Recorded because the principle was already written down and applied elsewhere in the same session. Knowing a rule and applying it are separate, and nothing mechanical closes that gap.

records.subject: feat(tools): a sweep for the class -- and it found a second instance on its first run
records.summary: api/sairndental/public-book.test.js asserted `reached || res.statusCode !== 400 || res.body.error.code !== 'NOTES_TOO_LONG'` for an arm titled "passes validation and REACHES THE NETWORK STAGE". Any one term satisfied it, and the request was 502ing before it reached anything -- because the block's resolveSlug stub throws unconditionally and public-book.js destructures it at module load, so NO arm in that block could ever get past validation. The arm was green the whole time

injection.unknown_reason: The arm and its harness stub appear to have arrived together, and no commit in the file's history shows the disjunction being ADDED to a previously-strict assertion. Recorded as unknown rather than attributed to the file's creation commit on a guess.

records.citation_note: The arm could fail, and could not fail for the state it described. Same end state as 1.1 -- an assertion that cannot go red when its claim stops being true -- reached through a disjunction rather than through decay.

contributing_factors.factor: THE ASSERTION WAS A THREE-WAY DISJUNCTION, SO ANY ONE TERM SATISFIED IT. `reached || res.statusCode !== 400 || res.body.error.code !== 'NOTES_TOO_LONG'` is green whenever the handler dies early, refuses with a 500, or refuses with a 400 carrying any other code. The arm already recorded its own claim exactly, in `reached`; the other two terms could only weaken it.
contributing_factors.action: Reduced to `assert.ok(reached, ...)`, with the observed status and error code interpolated into the failure message so the next reader gets the diagnosis rather than a bare false.

contributing_factors.factor: THE HARNESS MADE THE ARM IMPOSSIBLE TO PASS HONESTLY, WHICH IS WHY THE WEAK PREDICATE WAS LOAD-BEARING. public-book.js DESTRUCTURES resolveSlug at module load, and the block's stub throws unconditionally, so no arm in it could get past validation -- including the one whose entire subject is getting past validation. The disjunction was what let it look like it had.
contributing_factors.action: The stub is switchable and exactly one arm turns it on; every validation arm keeps the refusal it relies on.

contributing_factors.factor: IT WAS FOUND BY A SWEEP BUILT FOR A DIFFERENT FILE, ON ITS FIRST RUN, over 330 suites. Nothing about this suite was suspected -- it was green, in an app with no open findings, and the title read correctly.
contributing_factors.action: tools/negated_status_assertion_scan.py, registered report-only in PURPOSES. Deliberately a READ-LIST: `!== <code>` is correct when the claim is that some OTHER lock answered, and no mechanical rule separates that from 'it got through'.

contributing_factors.factor: A GREEN ARM WITH A TRUE-SOUNDING TITLE IS THE HARDEST KIND TO DOUBT. 'passes validation and reaches the network stage' is exactly what a reader wants to be true, and the only thing contradicting it was a status code nobody printed.
contributing_factors.action: The failure message prints the status and the error code, so the arm cannot fail without saying which stage it stopped at.

records.recurrence_open: The sweep finds `!== <literal status>` inside an asserting line. It does NOT find `assert.notStrictEqual(code, 401)`, which is the same claim with no literal operator, and it cannot see a disjunction whose weak term is not a status comparison at all -- `reached || somethingElse` would be invisible. It found this one because one term happened to carry the shape it scans for.

records.subject: fix(sabotage-check): the uniqueness guard was Python-only, and the first fix over-credited
records.summary: tools/sabotage_control_check.py's uniqueness guard -- the criterion added 2026-09-15 precisely because the tool had been under-crediting its best-written controls -- matched only the Python spelling str.count(old) != 1. JavaScript has no str.count, so the same guard written as s.split(anchor).length - 1 matched nothing, and tests/sairnbiz_po_recv_mutation_control.js was reported UNGUARDED on the day it was written despite guarding three ways: uniqueness, difference, and reading the mutated bytes back off disk. The same inverted signal as the 2026-09-15 finding, recurring in another language. The difference patterns were also lower-case only, so a JS control holding the original in a const named ORIGINAL was invisible.

injection.subject: feat(tooling): the negative-control recombination -- and the tool measuring the class was under-crediting its best members

records.citation_note: 1.1 is about a check that stopped checking. This one never checked the JS population at all rather than ceasing to -- it is the same end state reached by never having arrived rather than by decaying, which is why it is recorded as arguable. The nearer relative is the document's own eighth cross-domain discipline about instrument drift, which is not a numbered process rule.
records.phase_note: The criterion was correct and its implementation was one-language. Not a design error -- the design decision (credit a uniqueness count as the strongest guard) is right and unchanged; what was wrong is that it was written as one regex for one language.

contributing_factors.factor: The uniqueness criterion was written as a Python idiom (str.count) and JavaScript has no equivalent, so the same guard spelled s.split(anchor).length - 1 matched nothing
contributing_factors.action: Added the JS spelling, narrowed structurally to a VARIABLE argument so a findings count on a literal is still reported

contributing_factors.factor: The 2026-09-15 pass that added the uniqueness shape was prompted by Python probes and every example it listed was Python, so the population it was checked against could not have exposed the gap
contributing_factors.note: A criterion added from five Python examples cannot be shown to miss a JS one until a JS one exists. The tool's blind lock had no JS uniqueness fixture because no JS uniqueness control had been written yet.

contributing_factors.factor: The first attempt at the fix ALSO accepted == and ===, which credited two probes falsely within seconds -- a restore assertion (after == original) and a guard quoted inside a string literal
contributing_factors.action: Equality is deliberately not accepted -- it cannot be told from a restore check by any pattern, because they are the same text -- and both shapes are now NEGATIVE fixtures so the over-credit cannot come back

contributing_factors.factor: Nothing makes a guard shape travel with the language it is written in; GUARDS is a flat list of regexes with no notion of which idiom belongs to which file type
contributing_factors.note: Splitting GUARDS per language would make the tool stricter in a way that is only useful once a third language appears. Recorded rather than built, since inventing structure for a population of two is the over-engineering this platform's own rules warn about.

records.recurrence_open: GUARDS remains a flat list of regexes with no notion of which idiom belongs to which language, so a third language's spelling of any accepted shape would be invisible the same way. The blind lock now carries JS fixtures for the uniqueness and difference shapes, which means the gap is closed for the two languages in this repo and not for the general case.

records.subject: fix(sairnbiz): a payroll week recorded for an employee who then leaves is reachable again
records.summary: A timesheet week recorded for an employee who was later DEACTIVATED became unreachable through the product -- not editable, not zeroable, not removable, and invisible in every panel -- while the row stayed in sb_ts, on the server and in the backup. rTS() rendered only status === Active and openTsModal() refused independently, so the documented removal path (correcting a week is a re-save) existed exactly as long as the employee did. Tier A payroll data in the one store the criticality register says has no other copy.

injection.subject: feat(sairnbiz): the timesheet gets a real way to record real hours -- the second half of the fix

contributing_factors.factor: One status check was doing two jobs. rTS() and openTsModal() both asked status === Active, which correctly refuses RECORDING a new week for a departed employee and incorrectly refuses CORRECTING a week already on the books.
contributing_factors.action: sbTsRoster() splits the two: a non-active employee appears for a week if and only if a row already exists for that employee and that week, and saveTimesheet() re-checks the same rule on the write path.

contributing_factors.factor: The removal answer was written as a property of the WRITE PATH -- correcting a week is a re-save -- and never traced through the only UI that can reach that write path. The sentence was true about saveTimesheet and false about the product.
contributing_factors.action: the criticality-register claim is now backed by 11 arms that drive the real panel, not only the writer.

contributing_factors.factor: tools/removal_path_check.py reads EXTRA_ACTIONS in api/_resources/*.js and structurally cannot see a client-side reachability condition, so it reported sb_ts accurately and could never have surfaced this.
contributing_factors.note: Giving the checker a view of client reachability would make it a second source of truth for what the UI does and would be wrong far more often than right. The gap is real and stays; it is named in the sb_ts baseline entry so the next reader does not mistake the checker CLEAN for coverage.

records.recurrence_open: Nothing checks that a record a product can WRITE stays reachable after the entity it is keyed to changes state. sb_ts is fixed; the same question has not been asked of any other keyed resource whose UI filters by employee, patient or vendor status.

records.subject: fix(audit-checkpoint): both refusal paths beat -- and the NEVER_BEAT I reported was my own stale read
records.summary: api/audit-checkpoint.js refused SILENTLY on both of its refusal paths. NOT_PROVISIONED (the checkpoint table is absent) and WINDOW_INCOMPLETE (a window could not be read in full) each answered 503 and returned WITHOUT a heartbeat, while the success path and the generic catch both beat. cron-watchdog classifies a job with no heartbeat row as NEVER_BEAT and its own message offers both readings because it cannot tell them apart -- so a job firing daily and refusing daily would have been indistinguishable from a job that never fires at all. Found by reading the file while investigating a NEVER_BEAT report that turned out to be historical.

injection.subject: feat(cron): item 54 -- something now notices when a scheduled job goes silent

contributing_factors.factor: The NOT_PROVISIONED and WINDOW_INCOMPLETE early returns answered 503 and returned without calling beat(), while the success path and the generic catch both beat.
contributing_factors.action: both refusal paths now beat with outcome failed and a detail carrying refused and retry_helps.

contributing_factors.factor: Four existing arms already drove both refusal paths and every one asserted the 503 and the error CODE -- the response, which Vercel throws away on a cron invocation. The heartbeat is the only thing that leaves the function and nothing asserted it.
contributing_factors.action: four new arms assert the beat itself, two of them controls so the arms are not satisfied by a handler that beats unconditionally.

contributing_factors.factor: The test harness modelled the checkpoint table and not sairn_cron_heartbeat, so beats fell through to the stub default, beat() swallowed the result by design, and no arm COULD have observed one.
contributing_factors.action: the heartbeat table is modelled and every beat is captured on db.heartbeats.

records.recurrence_open: Nothing sweeps for cron endpoints whose refusal paths return without beating. api/audit-checkpoint.js is fixed; the same question has not been asked of /api/alf-alerts, /api/sairndental/send-reminder or /api/cron-watchdog, all of which use the same beat() helper and all of which have early returns.

records.subject: fix(sd-agent): the only AI endpoint on the platform with no budget
records.summary: api/sd-agent.js drove up to MAX_ITERATIONS model calls per request with no budget check at all -- the only AI endpoint on the platform not consuming the shared daily limiter

injection.subject: Add StoneDesk Agent SDK (sd-store.js + sd-agent.js) — tool-calling agent for profile/slabs/memory, write_slab confirm-first, verified end-to-end on preview.

records.citation_note: The process rules are about checks, documents and coordination. None of them covers a cost control that was never wired, and inventing a citation to fill the field is the exact thing `not-citable` exists to prevent.

contributing_factors.factor: The limiter is opt-in per endpoint -- each caller requires and calls checkAiRateLimit itself -- so adding an AI endpoint without one produces a working endpoint and no signal of any kind.
contributing_factors.action: tools/retry_backoff_check.py now treats checkAiRateLimit as breaker vocabulary, so a model-calling loop without one reads as unprotected in the sweep rather than as absent.

contributing_factors.factor: The other two AI endpoints are metered, so a reader checking whether the platform meters AI calls finds that it does. Two of three doing the right thing is what made the third invisible.
contributing_factors.action: The budget is consumed PER MODEL CALL here rather than per request, and the test asserts that count, because charging one unit for a request that can cost ten would have reported a healthy day while this endpoint spent ten times its share.

contributing_factors.factor: A limiter that fails OPEN is indistinguishable, at the call site, from one that decided to allow. The absence of a decision looks like a decision.
contributing_factors.action: `degraded` is carried out on every terminal status and surfaced rather than swallowed, the way api/claude.js surfaces it, and an arm asserts a healthy limiter reports it FALSE so the flag discriminates.

records.recurrence_open: Nothing prevents the NEXT AI endpoint being written without a limiter. The sweep reports it only if the model call sits inside a loop it recognises; a single-shot AI endpoint with no budget would not appear at all, and there is still no registry that says which endpoints must meter.
